newsitem.title: USA: Kevorkian charged with assisting suicides again.
newsitem.headline: Kevorkian charged with assisting suicides again.

text.p: Dr. Jack Kevorkian, the assisted-suicide crusader acquitted in three previous trials, was charged again on Thursday along with two others with crimes linked to 10 suicides since June.
The retired 68-year-old pathologist branded his accuser, Oakland County Prosecutor Richard Thompson, a "Nazi" and promised a hunger strike if he was jailed.
Kevorkian and his lawyer Geoffrey Fieger marched out of a courtroom after a judge granted his release on $50,000 bond.
"(Either) I die or the legal system gets out of this," Kevorkian told County Judge Edward Avadenka.
In granting bail, the judge refused the prosecutor's request that Kevorkian's release be conditioned on him not assisting in any more suicides.
"This is not going to be the court that will make a martyr out of Dr. Kevorkian," Avadenka said.

Kevorkian has admitted helping 44 people die since 1990 and has been the leading U.S. advocate for physician-assisted suicide. He has been tried and acquitted three times on related charges since 1994.

The latest charges involve 10 suicides in which Kevorkian assisted since June 20, including the controversial July 9 suicide of Rebecca Badger. In that case the issue of whether Badger was terminally ill when she died was challenged by the medical examiner.
Charged along with Kevorkian in several of the assisted suicides were George Reding and Neal Nicol. Nicol's home was used in at least one assisted suicide.
The three were also charged with moving the victims' bodies without permission of the medical examiner.

Kevorkian was also charged with possession of a controlled substance, listed as less than 25 grams of secobarbital, and with holding himself out to be a practicing physician while engaging in unlawful conduct. Kevorkian no longer has a medical license.
